subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, prove that r₁/(bc) + r₂/(ca) + r₃/(ab) = 1/r − 1/(2R).

mark_split.label: Write one term in half angles
Cancel to a sum of squares

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

steps.label: Write one term in half angles
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Substitute r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2) and b, c by the sine rule, then cancel. Write ONE term with a sigma; the other two follow by symmetry.

recall.must_convey: That r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2) and b = 2R sinB are substituted, and sinB expanded into half angles.
accept: substitute r one as four R sin half A cos half B cos half C and the sides by the sine rule then expand the sines into half angles
write everything in half angles and cancel
use the standard form of r one and the sine rule
r one ni half angles lo rasi, sides ni sine rule tho marchali
convert one term into half angles

steps.why: The whole identity lives in half angles, so converting everything at once is cheaper than converting piecemeal. The sigma is what stops the working tripling in length.
common_mistakes: Writing r₁ with cos(A/2) instead of sin(A/2).
Expanding all three terms in full and running out of space.

steps.label: Cancel to a sum of squares
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The cos(B/2) and cos(C/2) cancel top and bottom, and what is left has sin(A/2) over 4R sin(B/2)sin(C/2) — which becomes sin²(A/2)/r.

recall.must_convey: That the cosines cancel and the denominator becomes r = 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), leaving (1/r)Σsin²(A/2).
accept: the cosines cancel and the denominator becomes r so it is one over r times the sum of sin squared half angles
multiply by sin half A so the denominator is exactly r
it becomes one over r times the sum of the three sine squares
cosines cancel ayi denominator r avthundi
the denominator turns into the in radius

steps.why: Multiplying by sin(A/2) top and bottom is deliberate — it manufactures the exact product that equals r, and nothing else in the expression would.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the sines rather than the cosines.
Not spotting that the denominator is r.

steps.label: Use the half-angle sum identity
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) = 1 − 2 sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) — the Unit 6 identity, quoted.

recall.must_convey: That the Unit 6 identity Σsin²(A/2) = 1 − 2sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) is quoted, and the product replaced by r/(4R).
accept: quote the identity that the sum of the sine squares is one minus twice the product then replace the product by r over four R
use the transformations identity then the standard product result
it becomes one over r times one minus r over two R
aa identity vaadi, product ni r by four R ga marchali
apply the half angle sum identity

steps.why: This is exactly Unit 6 answer 27.1, quoted rather than re-proved — and r = 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) rearranges to give the product directly.

steps.label: Expand and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Multiply the 1/r through the bracket; the r in the second term cancels, leaving 1/(2R).

recall.must_convey: That multiplying out gives 1/r − 1/(2R), with the r cancelling in the second term.
accept: multiply through and the r cancels in the second term leaving one over r minus one over two R
expanding gives the required right hand side
the r cancels so it is one by r minus one by two R
r cancel ayi one by r minus one by two R vasthundi
the answer is one over r minus one over two R

steps.why: The r cancelling in the second term is what leaves a pure 1/(2R) with no r in it — which is exactly the form the question asked for.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the r in the wrong term.
